summary: Today’s pulse tracks Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution, governor says, Shop clerk and son charged with selling illegal kratom after two Ole Miss students die from suspected overdoses, and Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv. Across BBC and Guardian, the strongest repeated signals are blanchard, kratom, and officers. In the background, Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast and TSA to prohibit airport security officers from sitting down while checking travelers’ IDs keep the wider picture in motion.

headlines.title: Tennessee prison chief to resign after Christa Pike's failed execution, governor says
headlines.description: Pike survived two lethal injections on Wednesday and is currently in critical condition in hospital.

headlines.title: Shop clerk and son charged with selling illegal kratom after two Ole Miss students die from suspected overdoses
headlines.description: Aidan Hamilton and Robert Strang died after apparently ingesting kratom product last month Federal authorities investigating the recent deaths of two University of Mississippi students have charged a store clerk and his son with selling an illegal kratom product, prosecutors announced on Friday. A drug taskforce in Mississippi had previously urged people to avoid kratom, an herbal substance that acts as a stimulant at low doses and a sedative at high doses, after authorities found packages of kratom derivatives while investigating the deaths on 21 September.

headlines.title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
headlines.description: The strike on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge comes after repeat attacks on another major bridge in Ukraine's capital.

headlines.title: Medical plane with 6 on board missing off Massachusetts coast
headlines.description: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.

headlines.title: TSA to prohibit airport security officers from sitting down while checking travelers’ IDs
headlines.description: TSA says rule change is meant to keep officers ‘alert’, but union says it ignores safety and ‘common decency’ US airport security officers who verify boarding passes and IDs ahead of security checkpoints will no longer be allowed to sit down while working. The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) was moving forward with this change in policy to keep officers “alert”, the agency confirmed recently.

headlines.title: Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s former husband says he was ‘shocked’ by death of her ex-partner
headlines.description: Ryan Anderson says he reached out to Blanchard’s father to offer support after apparent overdose death of Ken Urker The ex-husband of Gypsy Rose Blanchard has said he was “shocked” by the recent death in Louisiana of her former partner Ken Urker – and that he would be there for Blanchard and her daughter “if she needs me”. Ryan Anderson made those remarks during an appearance on The Sarah Fraser Show podcast on Friday, providing a noteworthy reaction to the latest chapter involving Blanchard, who achieved an unusual level of celebrity after spending time imprisoned for a role in the murder of her abusive mother.

headlinePool.title: Women given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on Oktoberfest amusement ride
headlinePool.description: Investigation revealed thousands of voyeuristic videos taken on Munich beer festival’s Teufelsrad, or Devil’s Wheel Women have been given free cycling shorts to prevent upskirting on a famous amusement ride at the Oktoberfest in Munich, after an investigation revealed tens of thousands of voyeuristic videos circulating online. The Teufelsrad , or Devil’s Wheel, which rapidly spins around while people try to sit on it for as long as they can, is one of the beer festival’s oldest rides. But many of the videos discovered by German journalists focus on women whose traditional dirndl dresses have ridden up, often showing their underwear.

headlinePool.title: Tories plan to extend cuts beyond £47bn previously pledged, leak reveals
headlinePool.description: Exclusive: Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith told party members last year he had discussed making further savings if they win next election The Conservatives are planning to make sweeping cuts beyond the £47bn announced last year if they win the next election, according to leaked comments by the shadow chancellor. Speaking last year when he was shadow business secretary, Andrew Griffith told Conservative members he and fellow shadow cabinet ministers had discussed making further cuts in “every part of government”.

headlinePool.title: Greece returns priceless relics – and suggests UK should follow suit with Parthenon marbles
headlinePool.description: Greek PM hopes handover of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria will persuade Britain that time has come for ‘truth, reason, justice and morality’ In a ceremony replete with the sort of fanfare usually reserved for great events, Greece and Bulgaria have formally exchanged “a treasury” of relics and bones, sealing a cultural deal negotiated over decades. The handover involved priceless religious objects removed from Greece at the height of the first world war, as well as remains thought to belong to Tsar Samuel, Bulgaria’s revered medieval warrior ruler.

headlinePool.title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
headlinePool.description: The man accused of trying to take over the Israel-bound jet is named as Hamam al-Hammami by several media outlets.

headlinePool.title: ‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain
headlinePool.description: Demonstrators take to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities ⁠after ​new legislation fails to pass Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid ⁠and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle ⁠a mounting housing crisis ⁠after ​government measures were struck down by the opposition. Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike ⁠after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in ⁠Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on ​Friday.

headlinePool.title: Michigan state police rule out claim that Larry Nassar was removed from sex offender registry
headlinePool.description: Eaton county prosecuting attorney’s office had said court ruling forced removal of Nassar’s name – but he wasn’t on list because he was imprisoned out of state Michigan has removed more than 20,000 entries from its sex offender registry, but convicted serial abuser Larry Nassar is not one of them – the former Michigan State University and USA Gymnastics doctor was not in that system, as a local prosecutor’s office claimed, because he was serving an out-of-state federal prison sentence, according to state police. On 9 September, the Michigan supreme court ruled that the state’s Sex Offender Registration Act (Sora) cannot be applied retroactively to cases involving offenses committed before the law’s relevant date. Michigan’s state police, as a result, removed more than 20,000 people whose offenses occurred before 1 July 2011 from the agency’s online sex offender database. Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

headlinePool.title: California’s new laws target workers’ biggest fear of AI taking their jobs
headlinePool.description: The state, which is home to many AI companies, is one of the first to roll out workplace regulations targeting the technology California’s laws aimed at protecting workers from the impacts of artificial intelligence could pave the way for broader workplace safeguards across the US as calls for regulating the technology mount. As the federal government goes hands-off on AI, California is taking the reins to address workers’ biggest fears. On Thursday, California governor Gavin Newsom signed a suite of new laws that ban bosses from relying entirely on AI to decide whether to fire workers, using it to predict employees’ emotional states or collecting neural data, meaning the information from electrical signals of someone’s brain or nerves. They also require companies to notify workers if layoffs were caused by AI and prohibit AI surveillance in workplace bathrooms.

headlinePool.title: Why has Brazil accused the US of election interference?
headlinePool.description: The Latin American country will vote for its next president, as Lula da Silva and Bolsonaro clash over sovereignty, security and ties with Washington.

headlinePool.title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
headlinePool.description: More than 50 protests are taking place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.
